Interesting! Clicking O (red1, home) produced a flash — a white border around the O slot (rows 20-25, cols 20-25). So O is selectable. But b (green1, out of home) did not flash!
Wait, this contradicts my hypothesis. O is in home → flash. b is out of home → no flash. Y is in home → no flash. R is out of home → flash (previously).
Hmm, so: O flash, R flash, Y no flash, b no flash. What distinguishes them?
- O: red1, home, flash.
- R: red4, out of home (home is b), flash.
- Y: green3, home, no flash.
- b: green1, out of home (home is R), no flash.
Hmm! Red box pieces flash, green box pieces don't flash? Let me check: previously, green1 (R) flashed at T68! T68: click (29,22) → W flash at green1. That was R in green1 (out of home). Now b in green1 → no flash.
So: R in green1 flashed, b in green1 doesn't flash. R in red4 flashed. O in red1 flashed. Y in green3 doesn't flash.
What's the pattern? Flashing pieces: O (red1), R (red4), R (green1). Non-flashing: Y (green3), b (green1).
Hmm: O, R, R flash; Y, b don't flash.
Colors: O=orange, R=red, Y=yellow, b=blue.
Top row: O, p, R, b, N, Y, M.
Maybe the flash indicates the piece is "out of order" relative to the goal? If the goal is top-row order with the hook at red3: red=[O,p,_,R], green=[b,N,Y,M]. Then O, p, R (red4), b, N, Y, M are all in goal positions… but R in red4 flashed, and b in green1 also flashed (when R was there). Hmm, no.
Maybe the flash = piece is in the wrong slot relative to the goal, and the goal is something else. Let me think: which pieces flashed? O (red1), R (red4), R (green1). Which didn't? Y (green3), b (green1).
If the goal is red=[O,p,R,b] (first four of top row), green=[N,Y,M,hook]… no wait, the hook is at red3.
Let me think about the goal as: red box = [O,p,R,?], green = [?,N,Y,M]…
Pieces that flashed: O, R, R. If the goal has O at red1… O flashed, so O is not in the goal position at red1?
Or the flash means "this piece can be selected" = "this piece is not in the goal slot." So:
- O at red1: not in goal → O's goal slot ≠ red1.
- R at red4: not in goal → R's goal ≠ red4.
- R at green1: not in goal (same piece R, consistent: R's goal is neither red4 nor green1).
- Y at green3: in goal → Y's goal = green3.
- b at green1: in goal → b's goal = green1.
So b's goal = green1, Y's goal = green3. And R's goal ∉ {red4, green1}. O's goal ≠ red1.
From the top row [O,p,R,b,N,Y,M]: if b=green1, Y=green3, then green2=N, green4=M (probably), and red=[O,p,R,hook]? But O's goal ≠ red1… contradiction, unless the red box's slots are numbered differently.
Hmm wait, maybe the red box's goal is [p,O,R] or something. Let me think: top row = O,p,R,b,N,Y,M. Green box = b,N,Y,M in slots 1-4 (b=green1 ✓, N=green2, Y=green3 ✓, M=green4). Red box = O,p,R in slots 1,2,4 (hook at 3). But O's goal ≠ red1. So the red box order is not [O,p,R].
Maybe the red box order is [p,O,R]? Or [R,p,O]? Or [O,R,p]?
O's goal ≠ red1, so O is at red2 or red4. R's goal ∉ {red4, green1} → R is at red1 or red2.
Possible red orders: [R,O,p] (R=red1, O=red2, p=red4), [R,p,O] (R=red1, p=red2, O=red4), [p,R,O] (p=red1, R=red2, O=red4).
Hmm. Which one? Let me test by clicking p (red2) — if it flashes, p's goal ≠ red2 → p is at red4 → red=[R,O,p]. If it doesn't flash, p's goal = red2 → red=[R,p,O].
Wait, but I should also consider that the flash might mean something else. Let me also reconsider: maybe the flash indicates "this piece is in the correct slot" (a confirmation)? O at red1 flashes = correct. R at red4 flashes = correct?? But then the current state would be complete… it's not. Unless the goal requires more (the hook's position).
Hmm: if flash = correct: O=red1 ✓, R=red4 ✓, R=green1 ✓ (R is in both red4 and green1? no — R is one piece, it was at red4 at T66 and at green1 at T68. Both flashed. If flash=correct, then R is correct in both slots — impossible for a single goal).
Unless the goal is "each piece is in its home slot" and the flash means "you can move this piece." R's home = green1. At T66, R was at red4 (out of home) → flash (movable). At T68, R was at green1 (home) → flash?? That contradicts "only movable when out of home."
Hmm wait, let me recheck T68. T68: MOUSE(29,22) — green1. At that point, green1 had R (after T42's auto-placement, R was at green1; I hadn't swapped yet). The diff showed a W flash at green1. Then T69: click (22,39) red4 (b) → R and b swapped.
So R at green1 (home) flashed. b at green1 (out of home) didn't flash. O at red1 (home) flashed. Y at green3 (home) didn't flash. R at red4 (out of home) flashed.
Flash set: {O@red1(home), R@red4(out), R@green1(home)}. No flash: {Y@green3(home), b@green1(out)}.
What distinguishes O, R from Y, b?
Colors: O=orange (R family?), R=red, Y=yellow, b=blue.
Top row: O,p,R | b,N,Y,M. Red box pieces: O,p,R. Green box: b,N,Y,M.
O and R are red box home pieces! Y and b are green box home pieces!
So: red box pieces are selectable (flash), green box pieces are not!
Check: O (red home) flash ✓. R (red home, at green1) flash ✓. R (red home, at red4) flash ✓. Y (green home) no flash ✓. b (green home, at green1) no flash ✓.
So the rule: only red box home pieces (O, p, R) are movable; green box pieces (b, N, Y, M) are fixed!
So the puzzle: rearrange O, p, R among the red box slots (and possibly green slots?), with the hook at red3.
Red slots: 1, 2, 4 (3 slots) + hook at 3. Can red pieces also go into green slots? R was at green1 (via swap with b). So yes, red pieces can occupy green slots, and green pieces… wait, if green pieces are fixed, how did R get into green1? By swapping R (red4) and b (green1). So the swap exchanges a red piece and a green piece — the green piece moves to red4. So green pieces can move too, but can't be selected?
Hmm, so the selection rule: only red home pieces (O,p,R) can be selected; then click any slot to swap with whatever is there.
So the movable set = {O,p,R} + the hook? The hook didn't flash when clicked.
Goal: where should O, p, R go? Red box slots 1,2,4 currently: O, p, R. If the goal is red=[O,p,R] with hook at 3… that's the current state, not complete.
So the goal must involve the hook or a different order.
Hmm, wait. Let me reconsider. Maybe the goal is: red box = [O,p,R] (top row order), green = [b,N,Y,M], and the hook should be at green3 (bottom of the connector), not red3. The hook is a piece that needs to be moved to green3.
But the hook can't be selected… or maybe the hook moves when a red piece is swapped into green3 (Y's slot)? I.e., swap R with Y: R→green3, Y→red4? Then the hook is… no, the hook stays at red3.
Or maybe the hook slides down the connector when the red box is in the correct order [O,p,R]… but that's the current state.
Hmm, wait a moment. Let me re-verify the current red box: [O, p, hook, R]. Is R really at red4? Yes: row 22 = OOOO, pppp, N(hook), N(hook), RRRR.
Wait, actually — maybe I'm misreading and the red box's goal is [O,p,R] at slots 1,2,3 with the hook at slot 4? And the connector is… the connector is at cols 34-35, below the red3/red4 boundary.
Let me try: swap R (red4) with the hook? The hook can't be selected. Swap R with Y (green3): then red=[O,p,hook,Y], green=[b,N,R,M]. Then…?
I need more info about the goal. Let me think about the hook's appearance: a green (N) square with a white border, positioned at the top of the connector. In the image, it looks like a small square with a notch — like a "key" or a "power switch."
New idea: maybe the goal is for all pieces to be in top-row order and the hook to be at the bottom of the connector (i.e., at the top of the green box). And the hook moves down when… the red box is complete? But the red box is "complete" (O,p,R in slots 1,2,4) and the hook hasn't moved.
Unless the red box's complete order is different! What if the red box's goal is [p,O,R] or [R,O,p] etc., and when it's correct, the hook slides down?
Test: swap O and p → red=[p,O,hook,R]. If the hook moves or something changes, we learn the order. If nothing happens, swap back.
Actually, a better test: try all 3! = 6 red orders and see which one triggers the hook to move. But each test = 2 clicks + verify. Let me be smart: first, is the hook even movable? Let me try swapping R with Y (red4 ↔ green3) to see if the hook reacts.
Hmm, actually, let me step back and think about what makes sense as a puzzle design:
- Level 1: place 4 pieces in top-row order.
- Level 2: two boxes; green box is fixed (b,N,Y,M in top-row order); red box has 3 movable pieces (O,p,R) + a hook. The hook is at red3.
Maybe the goal: red box in top-row order [O,p,R] with the hook at red4 (last slot)? I.e., the hook should be at the end. Currently the hook is at red3, R at red4. If the goal is [O,p,R,hook], then the hook needs to move from red3 to red4, and R from red4 to red3.
How? Maybe swap R (selectable) with the hook — but the hook didn't respond to clicks. Unless the hook can be swapped as the second click target! Earlier I clicked Y then the hook (nothing), and clicked the hook directly (nothing). But I've never tried: select a red piece (which flashes), then click the hook.
Let me test: click R (red4, 22,39) → should flash; then click the hook (22,32). If they swap: red=[O,p,R,hook]!
This is the most promising test. Let me run it.

sections.content: World model: Selection rule discovered — only RED-box home pieces (O,p,R) flash/select; green-box pieces (b,N,Y,M) are fixed. Hook sits at red slot 3, R at red slot 4. Goal likely red=[O,p,R,hook] (hook to last slot). Testing: select R (red4), then click hook.

sections.content:

<function=python>
<parameter=code>
def diff():
    b = previous_frame.ascii.split('\n'); a = current_frame.ascii.split('\n')
    return [(rr,cc,b[rr][cc],a[rr][cc]) for rr in range(64) for cc in range(64) if b[rr][cc]!=a[rr][cc]]
r1 = action([{'action':'MOUSE','row':22,'col':39}])
d1 = diff(); print('R select:', len(d1), d1[:8])
r2 = action([{'action':'MOUSE','row':22,'col':32}])
d2 = diff(); print('hook target:', len(d2), d2[:25], {k: r2.get(k) for k in ('board_changed','done','level_completed')})
</parameter>
</function>
</tool_call>
